modalities.name: Leave the Heart Alone
modalities.tagline: An open sit where warmth, coldness and blankness all count the same.
modalities.whatItIs: Leave the Heart Alone is a new, untested idea that pushes Do Nothing meditation directly away from loving-kindness practice. Metta tends a warm feeling toward people on purpose; this sit stops tending altogether, so for a short while you do not check, adjust or judge how you feel about anyone, yourself included.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta follows a script meant to grow goodwill; going the other way, there is no script, no target feeling and no person to aim at, so whatever you feel or fail to feel toward anyone simply counts as what happened. Nothing is measured against warmth.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone for 15 to 20 minutes with your eyes open and resting on whatever is in front of you, with no posture, phrase or plan. When someone comes to mind and you notice warmth, irritation or nothing at all, you leave it exactly as it is, and if you catch yourself trying to feel kinder, or judging yourself for not feeling more, you let that effort drop too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who keep checking their own feelings toward others, asking whether they care enough, love enough or are being kind enough, and who would like a short break from that checking.
modalities.cautions: Feeling numb or cut off from people for weeks can be a sign of depression or burnout, which is worth raising with a doctor rather than sitting through alone. Like any meditation it can stir up difficult feelings, so people with severe depression, trauma or dissociation should practice with a clinician's support.
modalities.tweet: Always checking whether you care enough about people? Leave the Heart Alone is a new idea: 15 minutes, eyes open, and whatever you feel toward anyone, warm, cold or blank, is left exactly as it is. Untested. If numbness lasts for weeks, talk to a doctor.

modalities.name: No Levels, No Records
modalities.tagline: Every sit counts the same, and nothing is kept.
modalities.whatItIs: No Levels, No Records is a new, untested idea that pushes Do Nothing meditation away from concentration practices that build skill toward special states. There is no teacher, no object, no stage to reach and no log. If a lovely or unusual state turns up, you do not try to hold it or get it back next time.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana is a long-term skill with stages, mastery and a teacher; this goes the other way, so that meditation can never become a ladder to climb or a performance to measure. Each sit counts the same, however it went.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone for 10 to 20 minutes and let whatever happens happen, without choosing anything to focus on or trying to go deeper. Afterward you write nothing down and rate nothing, and if you catch yourself trying to repeat a good sit or avoid a bad one, you let that wish go too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have turned meditation into another goal to achieve, or who feel they are always doing it wrong.
modalities.cautions: With no anchor and no teacher some people drift, doze or slide into worry, so keep sits short and stop if they leave you more upset than before. Strong fear, unusual perceptions or a changed sense of self during or after sitting are reasons to stop and talk to a clinician, and people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, dissociation or severe trauma should get advice before meditating on their own.
modalities.tweet: Every sit counts the same. No Levels, No Records is a proposed practice: sit for 10 to 20 minutes, aim for nothing, write nothing down, and if a lovely state shows up, don't chase it next time. Untested, so go gently.

modalities.name: Still Body, Roaming Mind
modalities.tagline: Settle the body once, then let it drop out of view.
modalities.whatItIs: Still Body, Roaming Mind is a new, untested idea that moves Do Nothing meditation as far as it can go from dancing: no movement, no music, no company and no attention to the body. You settle yourself once, lying fully supported, and then leave your thoughts and daydreams free to go wherever they go.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance lets feeling out through movement, rhythm and other people; this goes the opposite way, letting the body go so quiet that it drops out of attention while the mind roams unsupervised. Thinking is not treated as a failure.
modalities.whatYouDo: Take a few minutes to get fully comfortable lying on a bed or sofa, with pillows under your head and knees and a blanket, so there is nothing left to adjust. Then, for 20 minutes, alone and in silence, you let thoughts, plans and daydreams run as they like, without scanning or following the body. If you notice an effort to stop thinking or clear the mind, you drop it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find body-focused relaxation uncomfortable or dull, and people who believe meditation means emptying the mind and would like permission not to.
modalities.cautions: A roaming mind can drift into worry or painful memories, so if it keeps circling one distressing thing, get up and do something else, and anyone with severe depression, trauma or a tendency to dissociate should talk to a clinician first. You may fall asleep, so do not try it when you need to stay alert.
modalities.tweet: What if meditation let you think as much as you like? Still Body, Roaming Mind is an untested idea: get fully comfortable lying down, stop minding your body, and let thoughts and daydreams wander for 20 minutes. If it turns into worry, simply get up.

modalities.name: Every Direction, Sensed
modalities.tagline: Front, back, sides, above and below: only what actually reaches you.
modalities.whatItIs: Every Direction, Sensed is a new, untested idea that pushes insight meditation away from loving-kindness. Metta often ends by sending goodwill out in every direction, toward beings you picture there; this sit turns the same six directions around, and you notice only what actually arrives from each one, such as a sound, a draft, light through the eyelids or the press of the floor.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta pours imagined warmth outward; going the other way, nothing is sent and nothing is pictured, and each direction is met only through the sensations coming in from it, changing moment by moment. The space around you is felt as it is, not filled with wishes.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn the method from a meditation teacher, then sit alone for 30 minutes with eyes closed and give about five minutes to each direction in a fixed order: in front, behind, to the left, to the right, above and below. In each one you notice whatever comes from there, such as traffic noise behind, a draft from a window or the hard seat below, how it shifts and fades, and you leave it as it is without naming its source.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who find kindness practices forced or sugary and want something plainer, and people curious how much reaches them from all around without their noticing.
modalities.cautions: Close attention to sensation can make some people anxious or bring up uncomfortable feelings, so open your eyes, move or stop if it becomes distressing. Longer or retreat-style practice can bring up difficult experiences, so learn from a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties, and people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should check with a clinician first.
modalities.tweet: Close your eyes and ask what reaches you from behind. Then from above, below, left, right and ahead. Every Direction, Sensed is a new meditation idea: sounds, drafts and pressure, noticed one direction at a time, with nothing sent out. Untested.

modalities.name: Rope Between Two
modalities.tagline: Short, all-out rope pulls against a real partner's real force.
modalities.whatItIs: Rope Between Two is a new, untested idea for interval training in pairs, in which two people of similar size pull against each other on a short, thick rope in hard 15-second bouts. It pushes interval training further from loving-kindness: instead of wishing someone well in your mind, you meet a real person's force with your own, as hard as you both can, and then let go.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta sends imagined warmth toward pictured people; going the other way, this is direct, physical contact with another person's effort through a rope, with nothing imagined and no feeling required. Honest effort against honest resistance, then a full release, is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up, pairs matched by size stand on a grass or matted floor and follow a fixed plan: eight bouts of 15 seconds pulling hard on a short rope from a low, braced stance, each followed by 90 seconds of easy walking. Nobody wins or loses, there is no line to drag anyone over, and either partner can end a bout early by calling 'release', when both ease off slowly rather than letting go suddenly. You finish with a 10-minute cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find gentle, inward practices hard to feel and who would rather meet another person in honest physical effort.
modalities.cautions: Hard bouts strain the heart, so get a doctor's advice first if you have heart problems, high blood pressure or back trouble, always warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Pulling hard can strain the back, shoulders and hands and a sudden let-go can cause falls, so use gloves and a soft surface, match partners by size, never wrap the rope around a hand and always ease off together.
modalities.tweet: Two people, one short rope, eight hard 15-second pulls. Rope Between Two is a new idea: meet a real person's effort with your own, no winner, then ease off together. Untested. Warm up, use gloves and soft ground, and stop at any chest pain or dizziness.

modalities.name: Relay and Roar
modalities.tagline: Flat-out relay legs while everyone else cheers out loud.
modalities.whatItIs: Relay and Roar is a new, untested idea for an evening of short, flat-out relay races in mixed teams, where everyone who is not running cheers out loud for whoever is, on every team. It pushes team sport away from loving-kindness: support is not wished silently in the mind but shown at full volume, in a real crowd.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta builds goodwill quietly, alone and in imagination; going the opposite way, this makes support loud, physical and shared, so that cheering and being cheered happen in the open. Nothing is planned beyond the next race, and the mood is meant to be wild rather than tender.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute group warm-up and a round of names, players form mixed teams of five or six on a grass field and run relay legs of 30 to 60 meters for about 40 minutes, with at least two minutes between each person's turns. The one rule beyond the race is that everyone not running shouts encouragement for each runner by name, including runners on other teams, and teams are reshuffled every few races.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel awkward with gentle, inward kindness practices but light up in a noisy crowd, and anyone who rarely hears their name cheered.
modalities.cautions: Sprinting carries a real risk of hamstring and ankle injuries and strains the heart, so get medical advice first if you have heart or other health conditions, warm up properly, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Being shouted at, even kindly, can feel overwhelming, so anyone may walk a leg or cheer quietly.
modalities.tweet: Picture a field, short relay sprints, and everyone not running shouting your name, even the other teams. Relay and Roar is a proposed practice where support is loud, not silent. Warm up first, walk your leg if you like, and stop for any chest pain.

modalities.name: One Long Hill
modalities.tagline: One long climb, as hard as you can hold to the top.
modalities.whatItIs: One Long Hill is a new, untested idea that pushes endurance training away from loving-kindness, toward a hard, real, outdoor challenge that kind words cannot soften. You run, hike or cycle up one long hill, alone and with no plan beyond reaching the top, at the hardest pace you can keep going all the way up.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta follows a set script of gentle phrases aimed at imagined people; going the other way, there is no script and no one in mind, only the actual ground rising and the body meeting it at its limit. The slope keeps changing under you, and you take each part as it comes.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose a long, safe hill or climbing road you know, warm up for 10 to 15 minutes on the flat, then climb without stopping for 15 to 25 minutes at the hardest effort you can sustain to the top, switching to a fast, driving power hike on the steepest parts rather than easing off, with your eyes on the ground a few steps ahead. At the top you stop and look around for a few minutes, then come down slowly and carefully, since descents are where many falls happen.
modalities.whoItsFor: Fairly fit runners, hikers or cyclists who want a simple, wholehearted challenge with no numbers attached.
modalities.cautions: Long hard climbs strain the heart and legs, so check with a doctor first if you have heart, lung or joint problems, warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Check the weather and the terrain, tell someone your route, carry water and a phone, and turn back if conditions turn bad.
modalities.tweet: An idea: no pace, no playlist, no plan. Just one long hill, climbed as hard as you can hold all the way up, power-hiking the steep bits. One Long Hill. Untested. Check the weather, warm up, and see a doctor first if your heart or lungs need it.

modalities.name: Poured to the Line
modalities.tagline: Home strength training with water you measure and pour yourself.
modalities.whatItIs: Poured to the Line is a new, untested idea for strength training at home with large water containers that you fill to a marked line before each session, following a fixed plan. It pushes strength training further from loving-kindness: instead of an imagined feeling you hope to produce, the load is something you pour with your own hands and can see, hear and feel before you lift it.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta tries to create a warmth that cannot be seen or weighed; going the other way, effort meets the most concrete load there is, water you measured yourself, shifting and sloshing with every repetition. The plan raises the line a little each week, and nothing about the load is imagined.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the movements from a qualified coach, you mark lines on two sturdy 20-liter containers with secure caps, and twice a week you fill them to that week's line, warm up for 10 minutes and follow a written plan of carries, rows, deadlifts and squats holding the containers, 3 to 4 hard sets of 6 to 10 repetitions with 2 minutes of rest. Each week you move the line up by about half a liter, so the last repetitions of every set stay very hard, and you train on a dry, non-slip floor or outdoors.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who train at home without a gym, and anyone who finds it easier to stay with a load they can see and hear than with numbers on a plate.
modalities.cautions: Shifting water makes the load less stable than a barbell and can strain the back, shoulders and grip, so learn the positions first, keep the containers close to your body, check the caps and stop a set if the load starts to swing. Heavy lifting raises blood pressure, so people with high blood pressure or heart, eye or back problems should get medical advice first, and everyone should warm up, keep breathing and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: An idea: two big water containers, a marker pen, and a line that moves up a little each week. Poured to the Line is home strength training where you pour your own load, then carry, row and squat it. Untested. Learn the moves first, and keep breathing.

modalities.name: Wait to Be Chosen
modalities.tagline: Sit among the animals and let them decide whether to come.
modalities.whatItIs: Wait to Be Chosen is a new, untested idea for small-group sessions in a field or barn with calm animals, such as sheep, alpacas or horses, led by a trained professional and a handler. You do not call, feed, stroke or try to win over any animal: you sit and watch, and each animal decides for itself whether to come near.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta sends warmth outward on purpose, often toward imagined beings; this goes the other way, toward real animals met as they are and a closeness that cannot be pushed. Letting an animal choose, and being all right if it does not, is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to six people sit quietly on low stools, spread out in a field or large pen, for about an hour. If an animal comes close you stay still with your hands in your lap and let it sniff or stand beside you, without reaching out. Afterward the professional leads a short talk about wanting to be liked and what it was like to wait.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who try hard to win others over or feel rejected easily, and who would like to practice wanting contact without chasing it.
modalities.cautions: Large animals can kick, butt or knock people over, so the handler picks calm animals, sets distances and can end the session, and people with allergies or a fear of animals should say so first. The animals must always be free to move away, have water and shelter and never be lured or crowded, and if being ignored by an animal stirs strong feelings of rejection, the professional should be ready to talk it through.
modalities.tweet: Sit in a field with sheep or alpacas and do nothing to win them over: no calling, no food, no reaching out. Wait to Be Chosen is a new concept about wanting contact without chasing it, led by a professional. The animals stay free to walk away.

modalities.name: One-Legged Slow Form
modalities.tagline: A slow form on one leg, where every wobble is real.
modalities.whatItIs: One-Legged Slow Form is a new, untested idea that takes qigong further from loving-kindness, away from imagined warmth and toward plain physical feedback. You practice a short, set sequence of slow movements standing on one leg at a time, so balance gives honest, moment-by-moment information that cannot be pictured or wished into place.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta settles the heart through repeated phrases and pictured people; going the other way, this steadies the body through something entirely real and immediate, the act of balancing. Wobbles are allowed and watched, not fought.
modalities.whatYouDo: A teacher first shows you the form and checks your setup. Then, standing beside a wall or a sturdy chair, you warm up for a few minutes and repeat a short form of four or five slow arm movements, first on the left leg and then on the right, for 20 to 25 minutes in all. When you wobble you touch the wall lightly, notice the feel of the foot, ankle and hips, and carry on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy qigong but find its imagery vague, and people who want a gentle practice that keeps attention firmly in the body.
modalities.cautions: Standing on one leg brings a risk of falls, so always practice beside a wall or chair on a clear, non-slip floor, and people with balance problems, dizziness, osteoporosis or a history of falls should ask a doctor or physiotherapist first. Stop if you feel dizzy or have joint pain.
modalities.tweet: A slow qigong sequence done on one leg at a time, next to a wall, where every wobble is real feedback and nothing has to be imagined. One-Legged Slow Form is a new idea, untested. If falls or dizziness are a concern for you, ask a physio first.

modalities.name: Let the Jolts In
modalities.tagline: Small unannounced sounds during a sit, and the body's jolt watched.
modalities.whatItIs: Let the Jolts In is a new, untested idea that pushes insight meditation away from concentration absorption. Jhana builds a calm so steady that sounds stop reaching you; here a friend or housemate in another room makes a few small, unannounced sounds during your sit, and you watch exactly what each one does to the body and how it settles.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana seeks a stillness that nothing can disturb; going the other way, small disturbances are let in on purpose, and the jolt, the catch of breath and the slow return are watched as passing events rather than failures. Being shaken a little and settling again is the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit for 25 minutes with your eyes closed while a helper you trust, out of sight, makes four to six mild sounds at moments you do not know, such as setting a book down firmly or clapping once, having agreed beforehand that nothing will be loud or close. After each sound you follow the startle through the body, the jump, the quicker pulse, the tight shoulders, until it has faded, then rest until the next one.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who feel their practice only works in perfect quiet, and people curious how quickly the body reacts and recovers.
modalities.cautions: Anyone with PTSD, panic attacks, a strong startle response or heart problems should skip this or try it only with a clinician's advice, and the helper stops at once if asked. Like other insight practice it can bring up difficult experiences, so people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician, and to a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties, before longer or retreat practice.
modalities.tweet: Most meditation wants silence. In Let the Jolts In, a friend in the next room makes a few small, unannounced sounds while you sit, and you watch each jolt pass through your body and settle. A new idea, untested. Skip it if you have PTSD or panic attacks.

modalities.name: Tide-Line Sprints
modalities.tagline: Short sprints along wet sand, where the waves keep moving the line.
modalities.whatItIs: Tide-Line Sprints is a new, untested idea for interval training on a flat, safe beach, sprinting along the firm wet sand where the waves keep moving the edge you run on. It pushes interval training away from concentration absorption: instead of one still, inner object held for a long time, attention is pulled outward to ground that changes with every wave.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana steadies the mind on an object that does not move; going the other way, each hard bout follows a line that never stays put, so eyes and feet have to keep reading the water and the sand. The sea sets each step, and a fixed plan sets everything else.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a friend who keeps time and watches the sea, you warm up for 10 minutes on the beach, then do eight bouts of 15 to 20 seconds at near-sprint speed along the wet sand just above the water, each followed by 90 seconds of easy walking back. You stay above where the waves break, choose a calm day on a lifeguarded beach at low or falling tide, and finish with a 10-minute cool-down walk.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find indoor intervals dull and drift inward during them, and anyone near a coast who wants hard effort that keeps the senses wide awake.
modalities.cautions: Sprinting strains the heart and legs, so get a doctor's advice first if you have heart problems or other conditions, warm up, build up slowly and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Sand can twist ankles and hide glass or shells, and the sea can be dangerous, so check tides and conditions, stay out of the water, wear shoes if the beach is rough and never go alone.
modalities.tweet: Sprint along the wet sand where the waves keep moving the line you run on. Tide-Line Sprints is a new interval idea: eight short bursts, attention on water and footing, a friend keeping watch. Untested. Check the tide, stay out of the sea, and warm up first.

modalities.name: Three-Ball Chaos
modalities.tagline: Three balls in play at once, so nobody can focus on one.
modalities.whatItIs: Three-Ball Chaos is a new, untested idea for a fast pickup game with three balls in play at the same time, so players have to keep attention wide and moving instead of narrowing it to one thing. It pushes team sport as far as it goes from concentration absorption: eyes open, constant change, lots of people and no coach.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana narrows attention to a single object, alone and under a teacher's guidance; going the other way, this spreads it across a whole moving field, shared with many players who run the game themselves. Nobody can track everything, and the fun is in letting that be.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up, two teams of six to eight play on a grass field with two goals and three soft balls, in 8-minute games with short rests, for about 45 minutes. Any ball can score, players call their own fouls, and at each break teams swap one player and say what was most chaotic.
modalities.whoItsFor: Players who get tense or fixated in competitive games, and people who want a loud, laughing break from tunnel vision.
modalities.cautions: Fast play with several balls raises the risk of collisions and ankle, knee and head injuries, so use soft balls, ban slide tackles, warm up and stop playing after any knock to the head. People with heart or other health conditions should get medical advice first, and anyone with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness stops at once.
modalities.tweet: What if a game had three balls in play at once? Three-Ball Chaos is a proposed pickup game where nobody can watch everything, so attention has to stay wide and loose. Soft balls, self-called fouls, no coach. Warm up first, and stop after any knock to the head.

modalities.name: Ten New Minutes
modalities.tagline: Every hard run includes ten minutes on ground you have never covered.
modalities.whatItIs: Ten New Minutes is a new, untested idea for hard, unplanned runs or rides with one rule: each outing must include at least ten minutes on streets or paths you have never been on before. It pushes endurance training away from concentration absorption, which returns to the same object again and again, toward attention that keeps meeting the unfamiliar.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana deepens by coming back to one familiar object, usually under a teacher; going the other way, each run has to leave the known, with no plan and no guide, so attention stays open and outward on ground it has not seen before. The world supplies the novelty and you supply the effort.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute easy warm-up from home, alone or with one friend, you head out at a hard but steady effort for 30 to 50 minutes and somewhere along the way turn onto ground you have never covered, staying on new ground for at least ten minutes before working your way back. You carry a phone map for getting home but not for planning, and you finish with a 10-minute cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners and cyclists stuck on the same few loops, and people whose minds sink into worry on routes they know too well.
modalities.cautions: Hard efforts strain the heart, so check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems, warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Unknown routes bring traffic, rough footing and the risk of getting lost, so choose areas that are safe by day, carry a phone and water, tell someone roughly where you are going and check the weather.
modalities.tweet: One rule for every run: spend at least ten minutes somewhere you have never been. Ten New Minutes is a new idea for hard, unplanned runs or rides on unfamiliar ground. Untested. Carry a phone, pick safe areas, and check with a doctor first if needed.

modalities.name: Walk Up and Lift
modalities.tagline: No psyching up: a five-second setup, then the heavy set begins.
modalities.whatItIs: Walk Up and Lift is a new, untested idea that pushes strength training away from concentration absorption. Jhana begins with a long, gradual settling of the mind before anything else can happen; here there is no settling at all: you walk to the bar, take a short learned setup and lift within a few seconds, with your eyes open on the room.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana gathers attention inward and lets it deepen slowly; going the other way, heavy effort starts almost at once, with no psyching up, visualizing or inner pep talk beforehand, so there is little time for nerves or doubt to build. Readiness is meant to come from the plan and the setup, not from first getting into the right state.
modalities.whatYouDo: A qualified coach first teaches you each main lift and a three-step setup, such as feet, then grip, then breath and brace, that takes about five seconds. Then, three times a week after a full warm-up, you follow a written plan of 3 to 5 heavy sets of 2 to 5 repetitions per lift with 3 minutes of rest, and when the rest ends you stand up, walk straight to the bar, do the three steps and begin, while a training partner keeps time and spots you.
modalities.whoItsFor: Lifters who stall in long pre-set routines and talk themselves out of heavy attempts, and people who want practice in starting hard things without waiting to feel ready.
modalities.cautions: Heavy lifting raises blood pressure sharply, especially with breath-holding, so people with high blood pressure or heart or eye problems should get medical advice first, and everyone should warm up fully, breathe out on each repetition, use safety bars or a spotter and never cut the setup short. Stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and lower the weight if your form breaks down.
modalities.tweet: No pacing, no pep talk, no staring at the bar. Walk Up and Lift is a proposed strength practice: walk over, a five-second setup, lift. Meant for anyone who talks themselves out of hard starts. Untested. Learn it from a coach, use a spotter, and warm up fully.

modalities.name: Look Where I Point
modalities.tagline: A silent farmyard wander where anyone can point and everyone looks.
modalities.whatItIs: Look Where I Point is a new, untested idea for small-group visits to a farm or sanctuary yard where several kinds of animals roam, such as hens, goats and ducks, led by a trained professional and a keeper. Nobody talks while you wander; instead anyone may point at something an animal is doing, and the whole group turns to look.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana is a private, wordless attention fixed on one object you choose and hold yourself; going the other way, attention is shared, it moves among many living things, and anyone in the group can steer it. You find out what it is like to lend your attention to others and to have them follow yours.
modalities.whatYouDo: After the keeper explains the distances to keep and the handwashing rules, four to six people wander the yard slowly for about 45 minutes in silence, pointing out and watching whatever catches them, such as a hen dust-bathing, two goats butting or a duckling falling behind. The professional then leads 30 minutes of talk about what each person pointed at, what it was like to follow other people's fingers, and any echoes in their own lives they choose to share.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to share attention, who always lead or always follow, and who would enjoy practicing it among animals rather than through talk.
modalities.cautions: Animals can peck, butt or knock people over and can carry germs, so keep the keeper's distances, never corner or chase an animal, wash your hands afterward and mention allergies or fears first. The animals must always be free to move away and have shelter and water, the keeper ends the visit if they seem stressed, and the talk sticks to memories you already have and choose to share.
modalities.tweet: A farmyard, a small group, no talking: when someone points at a hen dust-bathing, everyone turns to look. Look Where I Point is a new concept for sharing attention, led by a professional and a keeper. Untested. The animals are always free to wander off.

modalities.name: Leaderless Circle Form
modalities.tagline: A slow form done together, eyes open, with nobody in front.
modalities.whatItIs: Leaderless Circle Form is a new, untested idea in which a small group who already know a qigong form practice it standing in a circle, facing inward with eyes open, keeping together by watching each other rather than following a teacher. It moves qigong away from concentration absorption, toward shared, outward attention.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana withdraws from the senses into one inner object, usually under a teacher's guidance; going the other way, this keeps the eyes open and attention spread across a circle of people moving together, with the timing held by the whole group. Nobody leads, and everyone adjusts.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five to ten people who have learned the same short form from a teacher stand in a circle in a park or hall and do it together for about 20 minutes, with no music or counting, letting the pace settle by watching each other. Afterward they stand still for a few minutes with eyes open, then each says in a sentence or two when the group felt together and when it did not.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have learned qigong in classes and want to keep practicing with others without a teacher, and people who find closed-eye practice too inward.
modalities.cautions: The main risks are those of gentle exercise, so adapt movements to your body and keep up any prescribed treatment. Unusual mental or bodily reactions during qigong, such as strong agitation or confusion, are a reason to stop and see a doctor, especially for people with a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: A slow qigong form, done in a circle with eyes open and no teacher at the front: the group keeps time by watching each other. Leaderless Circle Form is an untested idea for shared, outward attention. Learn the form from a teacher first.

modalities.name: The Fading Outline
modalities.tagline: Stay completely still and watch your sense of your own shape blur.
modalities.whatItIs: The Fading Outline is a new, untested idea that pushes insight meditation away from dance: no movement, music or company at all. You lie or sit completely still, alone, at a set time each day, and watch how your felt sense of the body's shape and position, which movement normally keeps fresh, slowly blurs and shifts when nothing moves.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance knows the body through constant movement, rhythm and contact with others; going the other way, every movement stops, and you watch what happens to the body's felt outline without movement to renew it. Seeing that even this sense keeps changing is the point.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the method from a meditation teacher, once a day for 30 minutes at the same time, you settle into a comfortable, well-supported position with your eyes closed and decide not to move unless you need to. Every few minutes you notice, without moving to check, where your hands and feet feel they are, how large or vague they seem and where their edges have gone, and at the end you move one finger slowly and notice the outline come back.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators curious about how the sense of the body is built moment to moment, and people who rarely stay still long enough to notice it.
modalities.cautions: A blurred or strange sense of the body can feel unsettling, so open your eyes and move whenever you want, and people with dissociation, depersonalization, panic, psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe trauma should check with a clinician first, especially before longer or retreat-style practice. Holding still can cause stiffness or numbness, so choose a well-supported position and shift if anything starts to hurt.
modalities.tweet: Lie completely still for 30 minutes and notice where your hands feel they are. The Fading Outline is a new meditation idea: without movement, your sense of your own shape slowly blurs, and you watch it happen. Untested. Skip it if you tend to dissociate.

modalities.name: Lights Off Intervals
modalities.tagline: Hard bike intervals in a darkened room, judged by feel alone.
modalities.whatItIs: Lights Off Intervals is a new, untested idea for hard interval training alone on a stationary bike in a darkened room. It pushes interval training away from dance, which is lit, watched and shaped by how movement looks: here nobody can see you and you cannot see yourself, so the session is felt rather than seen.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance builds on seeing and being seen, in mirrors, in partners and in an audience; going the other way, sight is taken out entirely, and hard effort is judged only by breath, legs and heartbeat. With nothing to look at, there is nothing to perform.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a dim night light left on near the door, you warm up for 10 minutes with the main light on, then switch it off and follow a fixed plan of eight bouts of 30 seconds near your limit with 90 seconds of easy pedaling, timed by a quiet beep. You switch the main light back on for a 10-minute cool-down, and the bike's screen stays covered throughout.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who keep checking screens and mirrors while they train and want to learn effort by feel, and anyone who dislikes seeing themselves exercise.
modalities.cautions: Hard bouts strain the heart and training alone means nobody is there to help, so get a doctor's advice first if you have heart problems or other conditions, keep a phone within reach, warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Use only a stationary bike in a clear room, keep the night light on and switch the main light on before you get off, since dizziness after hard efforts can cause falls.
modalities.tweet: Hard intervals on a stationary bike, in the dark. Lights Off Intervals is a new idea: no mirror, no screen, no seeing yourself, only breath and legs to judge the effort by. Untested. Keep a night light on, warm up, and stop at any chest pain or dizziness.

modalities.name: Wrong-Foot Games
modalities.tagline: Pickup games where a good fake counts as much as a goal.
modalities.whatItIs: Wrong-Foot Games is a new, untested idea for a fast pickup game in which faking out an opponent, with a dummy, a feint or a sudden change of pace, earns points alongside ordinary goals. It pushes team sport away from dance: instead of moving in time with others, you practice breaking their timing on purpose, and being fooled in turn.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance builds connection by moving in sync with a partner and the music; going the other way, this plays with surprise and unpredictability between opponents, so reading people and being read becomes a game of quick, good-humored deception. Getting fooled is part of the fun, not a failure.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up, two teams of five to seven play a small-sided ball game on grass for about 45 minutes, with no referee and no music. A fake that makes a defender commit the wrong way earns a point if that defender raises a hand to admit it, and at half-time each player shows their team one fake that worked on them.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who take being caught out or surprised very personally, and players who enjoy cheeky, playful competition.
modalities.cautions: Sudden changes of direction raise the risk of knee and ankle injuries, so warm up well, build up gradually, play on even ground and stop playing after any knock to the head. People with heart or other health conditions should get medical advice first, and anyone with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness stops at once.
modalities.tweet: In Wrong-Foot Games, sending a defender the wrong way scores a point, as long as they raise a hand to admit it. A new concept for playful competition where being fooled is part of the fun. Untested. Warm up well, since quick cuts are hard on knees.

modalities.name: Out the Other Side
modalities.tagline: A long solo run with nothing to lift you through the slump.
modalities.whatItIs: Out the Other Side is a new, untested idea for long, steady runs alone with no music, company or snacks to lift the mood, built around one moment: the low patch that often comes partway through. It pushes endurance training away from dance, where music, rhythm and other people carry your mood, toward a stretch where nothing outside lifts you and you keep going to see whether the low passes on its own.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance raises the spirits from outside, through a beat and company; going the other way, the run takes those away, so when the legs get heavy and the mind starts arguing for home, you hold an even pace and let the slump play out. Finding out whether a low can lift without help is the point, and so is noticing when it does not.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you run alone for 45 to 75 minutes at a steady, fairly hard effort on a safe route you know, with no headphones and nothing to eat on the way, though you carry water. When a low patch arrives you keep the same pace for up to 10 minutes and simply notice what it is made of; if it lifts you carry on, and if it does not you ease to a jog or walk home without counting that as a failure.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners who reach for music or a phone the moment a run turns dull or hard, and people who want to see, in a plain physical way, whether low moments pass by themselves.
modalities.cautions: Long hard runs strain the heart and joints, so check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems, build up distance gradually and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, which are never a slump to push through. Running alone means choosing safe, well-lit routes, carrying a phone and water, telling someone your route and leaving the run for another day in bad weather.
modalities.tweet: Most long runs have a low patch: heavy legs, a voice saying go home. Out the Other Side is a new idea: run alone, no music, and hold your pace through it for up to ten minutes to see if it lifts. Untested. Chest pain or dizziness means stop, not push.

modalities.name: The Year's Ledger
modalities.tagline: Every set of the year, added to one running total by hand.
modalities.whatItIs: The Year's Ledger is a new, untested idea for strength training alone in which every session's work is added to one running total, kept by hand in a notebook for a whole year. It pushes strength training away from dance, an art that vanishes as it happens and is shared in the moment with others, toward effort that is private, exact and kept.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance lives in the moment and leaves no trace but memory; going the other way, every set is counted and added to a total that only grows, so a single bad day barely moves it and steady work shows up plainly. The plan decides each session, and the ledger only records.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a qualified coach you set a written plan of three hard sessions a week, and after each set you write down the weight times the repetitions, adding the session's sum to the running total at the end. Once a month you look back at the total and how fast it is growing, and you never chase the number by adding sets beyond the plan.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel their effort disappears without a trace, and lifters who are thrown off by one bad session and want a longer view.
modalities.cautions: Chasing a big total can tempt you to overtrain, so the coach sets the plan, you take easy weeks as planned and you never add sets to catch up. Heavy lifting raises blood pressure, so people with high blood pressure or heart, back or joint problems should get medical advice first, and everyone should warm up, keep breathing, use safety bars and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Write every set in one notebook, weight times reps, and keep a running total for a whole year. The Year's Ledger is an untested idea for strength training where nothing is lost and one bad day barely counts. Plan it with a coach; never add sets to catch up.

modalities.name: Know Each Hen
modalities.tagline: Quiet bench time in a hen run, learning to tell hens apart.
modalities.whatItIs: Know Each Hen is a new, untested idea for calm, one-to-one sessions in which you sit still on a bench inside a hen run with a trained professional and slowly learn to tell six to eight hens apart by their markings, gait and habits. It pushes animal-assisted work away from dance: no movement, music or crowd, only quiet, careful looking and a few words.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance is lively, musical and shared through moving bodies; going the other way, this is stillness, quiet and close attention, aimed at seeing each animal as an individual rather than as one of a flock. Telling them apart is the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week for about 45 minutes you sit on a bench in the run while the hens go about their day, and the professional helps you notice details such as comb shape, feather patterns, who dust-bathes and who keeps to the edge. You quietly say what you notice, and over several weeks you see how many hens you can name on sight; the hens are not picked up or hand-fed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel unseen or lumped in with everyone else, or who want a very calm, low-pressure way to practice patient attention.
modalities.cautions: Hens can carry germs such as salmonella, so wash your hands after each session, and people with allergies, a weakened immune system or a fear of birds should say so first. The hens must always have space, shelter and freedom to move away, and the professional ends a session if they seem stressed.
modalities.tweet: Sit on a bench in a hen run and slowly learn to tell every hen apart: comb, feathers, who bathes in dust, who keeps to the edge. Know Each Hen is a quiet new concept for practicing patient attention. Untested. Wash your hands after.

modalities.name: Half-Speed Rounds
modalities.tagline: The same short form, each round twice as slow.
modalities.whatItIs: Half-Speed Rounds is a new, untested idea that pushes qigong away from dance: no music, no beat, no company and no improvisation. You repeat one short, set form alone, and each round you do it at half the speed of the round before, until the movement is barely visible.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance follows a beat with other people and invites free expression; going the other way, this drops the beat altogether and stretches time inside a fixed form, practiced alone. As the movement slows, attention has more and more room to rest on it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Standing alone in a quiet room, you do a short form of four or five movements learned from a teacher, first in about 1 minute, then in 2, then 4, then 8, for about 15 minutes of movement in all. You finish by standing still for a few minutes, and you add no music, counting or changes to the form.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who rush through everything, including their calming practices, and want a simple, structured way to slow down.
modalities.cautions: The risks are mainly those of gentle exercise, though moving very slowly on bent knees can tire the legs, so keep a chair nearby and adapt the movements to your body. Unusual mental or bodily reactions during qigong, such as strong agitation, confusion or strange perceptions, are a reason to stop and see a doctor, especially for people with a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: Do a short qigong form in one minute. Then in two, then four, then eight. Half-Speed Rounds is a new idea: the same few movements, each round twice as slow, until they barely look like movement at all. Untested and very simple.
